Brooklyn immigration medical exam prices: two offices advertising $300

Quick answer

Two Brooklyn offices publicly list a $300 price for an immigration medical exam or booking. That does not establish that both visits have the same all-in cost. Michael Yuryev, DO, expressly says laboratory work, vaccines, and X-rays when required cost extra. Latina Medical's public booking page lists a $300 immigration medical exam appointment but does not establish the total cost of every necessary follow-up service. Ask each office for an itemized quote before scheduling.

This is an independent educational comparison. Neither provider is presented as an advertiser, a paid referral destination, a ranked recommendation, or a clinic that has agreed to call you back through this website.

What to bring

Ask the civil surgeon's office which photo ID, vaccination records, current Form I-693 version, and other medical or immigration documents are required for your specific appointment. The official USCIS Form I-693 instructions govern the process; a clinic checklist is helpful but does not replace current USCIS requirements.

The visit and sealed paperwork

  1. Use the USCIS Find a Civil Surgeon tool to confirm the individual clinician's eligibility.
  2. Request the appointment price and every expected lab, vaccine, imaging, follow-up, and paperwork fee.
  3. Confirm which records to bring and whether any tests must be completed before the I-693 can be finalized.
  4. Ask when and how the completed sealed packet will be available and how corrections are handled.

Five questions to ask before booking

  • Is the $300 for the complete exam visit, and exactly what is excluded?
  • What would common required tests or vaccines add for someone without usable records?
  • Which designated civil surgeon will sign the form, and can I verify that individual through USCIS?
  • How many visits are normally needed, and what can delay the sealed packet?
  • Are corrections, replacements, mailing, or pickup included in the quoted price?

How can you turn two advertised prices into comparable quotes?

Use a separate worksheet for each office. Copy the advertised exam price, the date you saw it, and the exact service description before calling. Then give both offices the same description of the records you have and ask the same questions. Do not fill an unanswered field with zero: an unknown lab charge is an unknown cost, not a free lab. The worksheet should distinguish a published statement, an answer from the office and an item you still need confirmed.

For Michael Yuryev's office, the published page answers one part of the comparison: physical examination and documentation are included in its stated price, while lab fees, required vaccinations and required X-rays are additional. Latina Medical's booking page gives the appointment price and duration but does not itemize those other components. That difference in detail is a reason to ask more questions, not proof that one office charges less overall. Keep each answer attached to its own office rather than carrying one clinic's exclusions over to the other.

  • Exam and documentation: what does the advertised appointment cover?
  • Laboratory work: is it billed by the clinic or by an outside laboratory, and when will you know the expected charge?
  • Vaccination review and any services the clinician determines are needed: which charges are included and which remain unknown?
  • Imaging, if required: where would it be performed, and who would quote and bill it?
  • Follow-up, paperwork corrections and packet collection: what does the office include and what may generate another charge?

What should you check about records before paying a deposit?

Make a list of the records you already possess before speaking with either office. Separate original records from copies and note anything you are still trying to obtain. Ask the office which documents it wants to review, whether it can clarify its document checklist before you book, and how it wants records delivered. Keep sensitive documents out of a general website contact form unless the practice has specifically directed you to an appropriate channel. This comparison does not review your records or determine which medical services you personally need.

Ask which individual clinician will perform or sign the examination and check that name in the official civil surgeon finder linked above. A business name, an advertisement and an appointment confirmation answer different questions; none should substitute for checking the clinician. If the office uses several locations, confirm the location attached to your appointment rather than assuming that a published address applies to every booking. Recheck any unclear information directly with the practice before making travel or payment commitments.

Which timing and payment details belong in the comparison?

The booking page's 90-minute appointment duration does not establish when a completed packet will be ready. Ask both offices about the expected sequence from the first visit through any follow-up and collection. Record which parts depend on records, results or another appointment. Treat the answer as the office's estimate, not a filing deadline guarantee. If timing affects an immigration matter, ask the appropriate qualified adviser about that matter separately; this price comparison cannot determine a legal deadline or filing strategy.

Before paying, ask whether the practice requires a deposit, when the balance is due, which payment methods it accepts and what its cancellation or rescheduling terms are. Ask how an outside laboratory or imaging bill would reach you if those services are needed. A payment policy can affect how much cash you need at the first appointment even when the eventual total is similar. Keep written price information and the booking confirmation together so you can identify exactly what was offered if you need clarification later.

How do you decide when one quote is still incomplete?

Compare the worksheets only after marking unanswered questions. If one office gives a detailed breakdown and the other gives only the appointment price, you do not yet have two equivalent totals. Ask the second office for the missing scope, or label its total incomplete. Avoid calculating a savings figure from different service bundles. You can still compare practical details such as travel, appointment times and the way each office explains its process, but keep those separate from a claim about the total medical examination cost.

Use the related medical exam cost guide to organize cost questions and the preparation guide to organize your document questions. Those guides support a conversation with the office; they do not replace current official instructions or a personalized quote. Stop the comparison when you have enough documented information to choose your next call, rather than treating either advertised price as a promise about your final bill.

Next steps and editorial method

We reviewed the two offices' own public prices and location information on October 28, 2026. Contact clinics directly for a personalized total and current designation. If you know of another Brooklyn clinic with a publicly documented I-693 exam price, send the source URL to the publisher via the site's contact page so the comparison can be considered for an update.

USCIS instructions say the applicant is responsible for exam costs, including required follow-up testing or treatment. This guide is not legal or medical advice, does not rank civil surgeons, and does not promise a result or immigration filing outcome.

faq.q: Do both Brooklyn offices quote an all-in $300 exam?
faq.a: No. Both publish a $300 appointment or exam price, but that does not establish equal total costs. Michael Yuryev explicitly excludes labs, required vaccines and required X-rays. Latina Medical lists the appointment price without itemizing those other costs. Ask each office for its own written breakdown.

faq.q: How can I check who will sign my I-693?
faq.a: Ask the office for the individual clinician who will sign and check that person through the official USCIS Find a Civil Surgeon tool. Do not treat the advertised business name or a booking confirmation as confirmation of current designation.
